paragraphs: More historical data does not always produce better forecasts. The authors find experimentally that appropriately shortening a time series can improve prediction accuracy. Their interpretation is that forecasting models can absorb noise and irrelevant fluctuations along with useful patterns, so a longer input may make the informative signal harder to extract.

They introduce Adaptive Masking Loss with Representation Consistency, or AMRC, drawing on information bottleneck theory. Its dynamic masking loss identifies especially informative temporal segments and uses them to guide training updates. A second component encourages consistency in the representations connecting inputs, target values, and predictions. Together, these components aim to focus learning while stabilizing the relationships the model needs for forecasting.

The reported experiments show reduced learning of redundant features and improved forecasting performance. The practical contribution is a training approach that prioritizes useful historical information instead of assuming that every additional observation helps. The finding concerns appropriate truncation and adaptive selection; it does not establish that shorter histories always yield better forecasts.
neurips-2025-abstain-mask-retain-core-ti.tldr: AMRC improves time-series forecasting by directing training toward informative temporal segments while keeping representations consistent.

paragraphs: Generated images can return to training datasets after being collected from the Internet. Repeated training on generated material can degrade image models, creating a reason to distinguish synthetic outputs from other images. BitMark addresses this identification problem for models that generate images through a sequence of bitwise token decisions.

The method inserts a watermark directly into that token stream during generation. It subtly influences individual bits to produce a signal that is detectable without visibly compromising the image. The authors report that this approach preserves image fidelity and generation speed while resisting a range of watermark removal techniques.

BitMark also exhibits what the paper calls radioactivity: a model trained on watermarked images can produce outputs carrying detectable traces of the watermark. These traces remain detectable even after fine-tuning diffusion or autoregressive image models on marked images. This extends detection beyond the original generator's outputs to evidence of subsequent training exposure. The contribution supports identifying generated content as a step toward preventing model collapse.
neurips-2025-bitmark-watermarking-bitwis.tldr: BitMark embeds detectable watermarks during image generation, with traces that can persist in models subsequently trained on the marked images.

paragraphs: Membership inference asks whether a particular example was part of a model's training data. For large vision-language models, existing approaches often depend on internal information, such as likelihood-based features. That makes them difficult to apply when a service exposes only generated responses and conceals its internal computations.

This paper proposes probing memory through those visible responses alone. The central distinction is between information a model could infer from general world knowledge and private semantic details associated with a suspected training image. The method calibrates its probing against prior knowledge, aiming to make recalled image-specific information more informative evidence of training membership.

Experiments cover four vision-language models and three datasets. The authors report effective identification of training examples in this black-box setting, with performance comparable to approaches using greater internal access. Additional analyses support robustness against the adversarial manipulations considered. These results show that withholding internal model features does not, by itself, eliminate the tested form of training-data exposure through generated outputs.
neurips-2025-black-box-membership-infere.tldr: The proposed attack identifies likely training images from visible model responses by probing private details beyond general world knowledge.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how the representation conditioning a diffusion model affects what it can generate. The authors argue that conditioning explains much of diffusion models' success, and seek representations that support accurate image modeling, are easy to generate, and can be recombined to create images beyond the training distribution.

Their Discrete Latent Code, or DLC, represents an image as a sequence of discrete tokens derived from self-supervised Simplicial Embeddings. These codes replace the usual continuous image embeddings as conditioning information. Their compositional structure allows codes to be combined so that a generator can bring together semantic content from different images.

The authors report improved generation fidelity and a new state of the art for unconditional ImageNet generation. They also demonstrate coherent combinations outside the training distribution. For text-to-image generation, they use pretrained language models and fine-tune a text diffusion model on 9 million image-caption pairs to generate DLCs. This shows how a shared discrete representation can connect text-driven code generation with an image generator.
neurips-2025-compositional-discrete-late.tldr: Discrete Latent Codes improve diffusion image generation and enable semantic combinations beyond the image generator's training distribution.

paragraphs: Poor illumination can obscure the visual information needed for object detection and segmentation. FRBNet addresses this by improving the features a network extracts from dark images. The authors begin with image formation, extending the classical Lambertian model to describe low-light conditions more fully than the modeling used in existing invariant-feature methods.

They then analyze images in the frequency domain, where the representation exposes patterns at different spatial frequencies. Under their formulation, they prove that ratios between frequency-domain channels can support illumination-invariant feature extraction through structured filtering. FRBNet turns this result into a trainable module that combines the channel-ratio operation with a learned frequency-domain filter.

The module can be inserted into existing networks without changing their loss functions, making the contribution applicable to multiple downstream tasks. Experiments report gains of 2.2 mAP for dark object detection and 2.9 mIoU for nighttime segmentation. These findings support the usefulness of modeling illumination within feature extraction, with the reported benefits demonstrated across the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2025-frbnet-revisiting-low-light.tldr: FRBNet uses frequency-domain channel ratios and learned filtering to improve low-light visual features without changing existing task losses.

paragraphs: Sign language translation depends on representing movement precisely, including small finger articulations. Geo-Sign focuses on the geometry of skeletal movement representations. Its motivation is that the hierarchical organization of sign-language motion may be represented effectively in hyperbolic space, giving the translation model features that better distinguish subtle movements.

The method first obtains skeletal features from spatio-temporal graph convolutional networks, which process relationships across body joints and time. It projects these features into the Poincaré ball, a model of hyperbolic geometry. A weighted Fréchet mean aggregates features in that geometry, while a contrastive loss shapes their relationships directly within the same space.

These components act as regularization within an end-to-end translation framework, guiding the representations used by the language model. The authors report improvements over state-of-the-art RGB methods alongside privacy and computational-efficiency benefits. The findings support the potential of improving skeletal representation geometry as a route to better translation, complementing efforts centered on the language model's capacity.
neurips-2025-geo-sign-hyperbolic-contras.tldr: Geo-Sign uses hyperbolic geometry to structure skeletal motion features and improve sign language translation.

paragraphs: Graph learning models are often evaluated on a small selection of academic citation networks, despite their intended use across many industries. GraphLand broadens that evaluation with 14 industrial graph datasets for predicting properties of individual nodes. The datasets vary in size, connectivity structure, and available features within a unified benchmark.

The benchmark also supports studying distribution changes over time. It covers both transductive and inductive settings, allowing researchers to examine temporal shifts under different conditions for applying a learned model. This matters especially for graph foundation models, whose proposed value includes transferring across datasets and application domains.

The authors compare graph neural networks with gradient-boosted decision trees, including trees supplied with additional graph-derived features. Those augmented tree models sometimes provide strong baselines. The evaluated general-purpose graph foundation models fail to achieve competitive results on these datasets. Together, the findings show why broader industrial evaluation can change the apparent strength of methods and why established industrial models deserve inclusion in comparisons.
neurips-2025-graphland-evaluating-graph-.tldr: GraphLand tests graph learning on 14 industrial datasets, revealing strong tree-based baselines and weaknesses in evaluated graph foundation models.

paragraphs: HiDISC tackles recognition when both the data domain and some categories can be unfamiliar at test time. Its setting excludes access to target-domain data during training. This makes the problem more demanding than category discovery methods that train with labeled and unlabeled examples drawn from the same domain.

The framework learns hyperbolic representations without repeatedly simulating training episodes. GPT-guided diffusion introduces limited but diverse variations of the source domain. A method called Tangent CutMix creates pseudo-novel samples through interpolation in tangent space, respecting the curved representation geometry. The curvature itself is learned so that the geometry can adapt to the dataset's complexity.

A combined objective aligns representations, applies hyperbolic contrastive regularization, and repels outliers to encourage compact semantic structure. The authors report state-of-the-art results on PACS, Office-Home, and DomainNet, outperforming the compared Euclidean and hyperbolic methods. The contribution brings domain variation and category novelty into one representation-learning framework while avoiding the episodic simulation used by the previous DG-GCD approach.
neurips-2025-hidisc-a-hyperbolic-framewo.tldr: HiDISC combines synthetic domain variation with adaptive hyperbolic representations to recognize known and novel categories in unseen domains.

paragraphs: InterMT studies how to align models for ongoing conversations that mix modalities. Such interactions require a model to understand interleaved context and respond coherently across multiple turns. The work is presented as an initial exploration, with expert human oversight playing a central role because current models struggle with these complex interactions.

The dataset records preferences at both the overall conversation level and more local levels across nine sub-dimensions. It contains 15.6 thousand prompts, 52.6 thousand multi-turn dialogue instances, and 32.4 thousand human-labeled preference pairs. To construct the interactions despite model capability gaps, the authors use an agentic workflow combining multimodal models with tools.

The accompanying InterMT-Bench evaluates models' ability to assist judges on multi-turn multimodal tasks. Applications including judge moderation demonstrate the dataset's utility, and the authors report a multi-turn scaling law for the judge model. The contribution supplies human-grounded preference data and an evaluation setting for studying interaction quality across exchanges, beyond the quality of a single isolated response.
neurips-2025-intermt-multi-turn-interlea.tldr: InterMT provides human preference data and a benchmark for evaluating and aligning multi-turn multimodal interactions.

paragraphs: Foundation vision encoders produce useful representations, but their feature maps often have low spatial resolution. Tasks that need detailed outputs across an image therefore require a way to expand those features. JAFAR is a lightweight feature upsampler designed to work with different foundation encoders and requested output resolutions.

Its attention-based module connects high-resolution queries with low-resolution keys carrying semantic information. Spatial Feature Transform modulation helps align the spatial representations involved. This arrangement aims to retain the encoder's useful semantic content while recovering the fine spatial detail needed for dense downstream processing.

A notable result concerns training without high-resolution feature ground truth. The authors find that learning at relatively low resolutions and small upsampling ratios generalizes well to substantially higher scales. Across the evaluated dense vision applications, JAFAR recovers intricate pixel-level detail and consistently outperforms existing feature upsampling methods. These findings make modest-scale training relevant to higher-resolution use, while supporting a reusable component for expanding the spatial usefulness of foundation-model features.
neurips-2025-jafar-jack-up-any-feature-a.tldr: JAFAR expands low-resolution vision features into detailed spatial representations, with training at small scales generalizing to larger ones.

paragraphs: Identifying a neuron's functional identity is difficult when large-scale recordings lack anatomical or molecular labels. NuCLR approaches this through recorded activity, treating a neuron's relationship to the surrounding population as useful evidence about its identity. The aim is to learn representations that capture more than an isolated activity trace.

A spatio-temporal transformer models both changes within each neuron's activity and interactions across neurons. Training uses a self-supervised contrastive objective to encourage representations that remain stable over time while distinguishing neurons. This connects the desired representation to persistent identity information rather than only momentary fluctuations in activity.

Across multiple open-access datasets, NuCLR outperforms prior methods on cell-type and brain-region classification. It also generalizes to entirely new populations without retraining or stimulus labels, and its performance scales effectively with data size. The results support population context as an important source of information for interpreting neuron identity, showing that activity recordings contain useful signals for both cell typing and localization.
neurips-2025-know-thyself-by-knowing-oth.tldr: NuCLR learns neuron identity from individual activity and population interactions, generalizing to new populations without retraining.

paragraphs: A plan can reach its goal yet violate requirements along the way. LexiCon evaluates this aspect of language-model planning by introducing temporal constraints into planning problems described in natural language. The motivation is that unconstrained planning benchmarks do not adequately test adherence to requirements that matter in real-world settings, including safety constraints.

The benchmark starts with existing planning environments, adds temporal constraints on their states, and translates the resulting problems into natural language for a model to solve. Its extensible design accepts new unconstrained environment generators and constructs constraints automatically. This provides a way to expand the environment collection and increase problem difficulty as model capabilities improve.

Experiments show that evaluated state-of-the-art models, including GPT-5, o3, and R1, perform worse as tasks become more constrained. The result highlights a gap between general planning ability and producing plans that satisfy additional requirements. LexiCon makes that gap measurable through a systematic family of constrained problems.
neurips-2025-lexicon-a-benchmark-for-pla.tldr: LexiCon tests natural-language planning with temporal constraints and finds that model performance declines as constraints increase.

paragraphs: MetaDefense addresses jailbreak attacks associated with fine-tuning, focusing on harmful requests concealed by attack templates. The authors observe that existing defenses struggle with previously unseen templates even when the model's embedding space contains information that distinguishes disguised harmful queries. Their approach aims to turn that information into an explicit defensive decision.

The framework checks interactions at two stages. Before generation, it predicts whether the incoming query is harmful. During generation, it evaluates partial responses so that an interaction can be stopped before more harmful content is emitted. Specialized prompts train the model to make both types of harmfulness prediction.

Experiments evaluate LLaMA-2-7B, Qwen-2.5-3B-Instruct, and LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct. The authors report substantially stronger defenses than existing mechanisms against both familiar and unseen attack templates, while maintaining competitive performance on benign tasks. The findings support combining request screening with monitoring of emerging responses, giving the defense opportunities to act at more than one point in generation.
neurips-2025-metadefense-defending-fine-.tldr: MetaDefense detects harmful queries before generation and monitors partial responses to stop potentially harmful interactions early.

paragraphs: Direct alignment methods such as Direct Preference Optimization train language models from preference data without a separate reward model. Nevertheless, their performance can worsen as training continues. The paper examines one attributed cause: offline preference data may leave the optimization insufficiently constrained, allowing probability to shift toward undesirable responses absent from that data.

The proposed IS-DAAs modify the training objective using an importance-sampling ratio that accounts for the reference policy's distribution. This reweighting is intended to mitigate the distribution shift arising during offline alignment. Because importance sampling can introduce high variance, the method caps the ratio at a maximum value.

Experiments show that the approach mitigates over-optimization and outperforms other methods aimed at the same problem, particularly when regularization is weak. The contribution is a modification to direct alignment objectives that addresses how training weights relate to the reference distribution. The empirical findings support this mechanism as a useful way to reduce degradation during continued preference training.
neurips-2025-mitigating-reward-over-opti.tldr: Clipped importance weighting helps direct alignment methods reduce distribution shift and the performance degradation caused by over-optimization.

paragraphs: Biologically realistic neuron models help connect cellular properties with neural behavior, but experimental responses naturally vary across trials. NOBLE addresses the difficulty of representing that variability alongside complex voltage dynamics. It learns a mapping from interpretable neuron features to the voltage response at the cell body following injected current.

The framework uses a neural operator and a continuous, frequency-modulated embedding of those features. Training data come from synthetic simulations of biologically realistic neuron models. NOBLE predicts distributions of neural dynamics, and interpolation within its embedding space produces dynamics consistent with observed experimental responses. This makes variability part of the generated behavior.

The authors validate generalization using real experimental data and report a 4,200-fold speedup over the numerical solver. The resulting synthetic neurons resemble experimental recordings and display trial-to-trial variability. These findings support a fast approach to generating biologically informed neural responses, with potential applications in larger circuit models and investigations of cellular computation.
neurips-2025-noble-neural-operator-with-.tldr: NOBLE rapidly generates biologically informed neuron dynamics that capture experimental variability, with a reported 4,200-fold solver speedup.

paragraphs: This paper studies language generation in the limit, a theoretical framework with several levels of generation capability. Its central question is whether combining collections that each permit generation preserves that capability. Such closure under finite unions holds for traditional learning tasks such as classification, making it a natural property to investigate here.

The authors prove that finite unions of generatable classes need not be generatable. The same failure can occur for non-uniformly generatable classes. A stronger construction combines a non-uniformly generatable class with a uniformly generatable one and obtains a union that is not generatable. Thus, successful generators for separate collections do not guarantee a generator for their combined collection.

The construction also resolves a question about uncountable classes by establishing a non-uniformly generatable class that does not satisfy the eventually unbounded closure condition. Carefully designed classes and a new diagonalization argument underpin the results. The implication concerns the limits of combining generators within this formal model, ruling out a general boosting principle based on union.
neurips-2025-on-union-closedness-of-lang.tldr: The paper proves that combining individually generatable language classes can yield a class that is not generatable.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes harder when an environment changes during learning. This paper studies communicating Markov decision processes whose transition changes have a low-rank component together with sparse changes. That structural assumption allows the algorithm to exploit coordinated variation instead of treating every transition change as independent.

The proposed SVUCRL algorithm tracks low-rank variation online and uses incremental robust principal component analysis to separate structured drift from sparse shocks. It also adjusts confidence ranges using a bias-corrected estimate of local variation and forecasts factors with a shrinkage center. These components connect estimates of environmental change to the learner's uncertainty.

The authors prove a dynamic-regret bound with separate contributions from ordinary learning, non-stationarity, and an additional transition-variation term. For low-rank drift, the non-stationarity contribution scales with the square root of the structural parameter K rather than the square root of the state-action count. The stated bound achieves square-root time scaling up to logarithms, improving on prior three-quarter-power guarantees under the studied structure.
neurips-2025-optimal-regret-bounds-via-l.tldr: SVUCRL exploits low-rank and sparse transition changes to obtain improved regret guarantees in non-stationary reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: The paper considers assigning jobs to machines whose processing times can differ arbitrarily across jobs. The objective is to minimize the largest machine load, called the makespan. Machines are strategic: they may misreport processing times to reduce their own load, so the scheduling mechanism must also make truthful reporting a sound choice.

Without predictive assistance, the best possible deterministic strategyproof approximation has a factor equal to the number of machines. The authors introduce predictions into this setting and show that only a number of predicted values proportional to the combined count of jobs and machines is needed. The resulting algorithm remains deterministic and strategyproof.

Its performance has two guarantees. Correct predictions yield a makespan within a constant factor of the optimum, while arbitrarily poor predictions still give a bound proportional to the number of machines. This separates the benefit of accurate predictions from the protection available when they fail. The contribution obtains stronger performance conditionally on useful predictions while retaining a worst-case guarantee.
neurips-2025-parsimonious-predictions-fo.tldr: A strategyproof scheduler uses O(m+n) predictions to achieve constant-factor performance when predictions are correct and O(n) protection otherwise.

paragraphs: Safety alignment for reasoning models must address harmful outputs while preserving their ability to solve complex, multi-step problems. SAFEPATH intervenes at the beginning of reasoning. It fine-tunes a model to produce a short, eight-token safety primer when faced with a harmful prompt, leaving the subsequent reasoning process unsupervised.

This concentrates training supervision on an early response cue rather than prescribing the full reasoning sequence. The authors evaluate whether that small intervention can influence the resulting output while maintaining reasoning performance. They also introduce a zero-shot variant that requires no fine-tuning and examine how existing language-model safety approaches transfer to reasoning-focused models.

Across multiple benchmarks, the reported results show reduced harmful outputs with maintained reasoning performance. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, SAFEPATH reduces harmful responses by up to 90.0% and blocks 83.3% of jailbreak attempts. It requires 295.9 times less compute than Direct Refusal and 314.1 times less than SafeChain. These are empirical results supporting a lightweight early-alignment intervention.
neurips-2025-safepath-preventing-harmful.tldr: SAFEPATH trains reasoning models to start harmful-prompt responses with a brief safety primer, reducing harmful outputs while preserving reasoning performance.

paragraphs: Generating additional training images requires preserving what makes an example belong to its class while introducing useful variation. Methods conditioned on both an image and text can struggle because the image representation also captures incidental details. Those details, such as environmental context, can conflict with text instructions intended to change them.

The proposed framework uses an image embedding model that emphasizes salient concepts and reduces the influence of irrelevant visual attributes during synthesis. This is intended to preserve features that distinguish classes while allowing text prompts to control other variations. The approach connects fidelity and diversity through the choice of conditioning representation.

Experiments across eight fine-grained vision datasets report stronger performance than state-of-the-art augmentation methods. Average classification accuracy improvements are 0.73% in conventional settings and 6.5% in long-tail settings. These findings support the value of generating variation around class-relevant content, with the larger reported improvement occurring when the training data have a long-tailed distribution.
neurips-2025-salient-concept-aware-gener.tldr: Salient concept-aware conditioning improves generated training images by preserving class-defining details while allowing controlled visual variation.

paragraphs: Selection based entirely on merit can still reflect differences in what candidates expect to gain from success. This paper models candidates from socioeconomic groups with different perceived post-selection values. Each chooses effort by weighing its cost against expected reward; that effort produces observable merit, which alone determines selection.

The authors characterize a unique Nash equilibrium in the large-agent limit. Their formulas connect valuation differences and institutional selectivity to effort, representation, welfare, and utility. They also propose a cost-sensitive optimization framework for assessing changes to selectivity or perceived value that could reduce disparities while preserving institutional goals.

The mechanism is perception-driven: different expected benefits can rationally lead groups to invest different amounts of effort before selection occurs. Social context, including AI-generated career or salary guidance, can shape those expectations. The model is static and represents one stage of a broader feedback cycle. Within that scope, it shows how apparently impartial selection can inherit disparities through the incentives candidates face beforehand.
neurips-2025-strategic-costs-of-perceive.tldr: A game-theoretic model shows how group differences in perceived rewards can create disparities even when selection depends solely on merit.

paragraphs: Video step grounding identifies which steps of a specified task occur in a video. Common approaches require labeled training examples and process the entire recording before making decisions. This paper studies a setting where predictions must be made online, without task-specific training or access to the whole video.

The authors first use the zero-shot capabilities of large multimodal models to identify steps from a restricted set of frames. They report that this basic online approach already outperforms evaluated offline, training-based models. They then introduce Bayesian Grounding with Large Multimodal Models, or BaGLM, to incorporate information from previously observed frames.

BaGLM uses Bayesian filtering principles to combine current predictions with a model of step transitions. That transition model includes a dependency matrix extracted using language models and an estimate of step progress. Experiments on three datasets show better performance than state-of-the-art training-based offline methods. The findings support combining pretrained visual understanding with temporal knowledge for step recognition as a video unfolds.
neurips-2025-training-free-online-video-.tldr: BaGLM combines zero-shot multimodal predictions with Bayesian temporal filtering to identify video steps online without task-specific training.

paragraphs: Video-R1 investigates reinforcement learning as a way to improve reasoning about videos in multimodal language models. The authors identify two obstacles to directly applying GRPO training: insufficient attention to temporal information and a shortage of high-quality video-reasoning data. Their approach addresses both the learning algorithm and the training material.

They introduce T-GRPO to encourage the model to use temporal information when reasoning about video. They also mix image-reasoning examples with video data. Two datasets support the process: Video-R1-CoT-165k for supervised initialization and Video-R1-260k for reinforcement learning. Both contain image and video examples, expanding training beyond video-only supervision.

The reported results show substantial improvements on video reasoning benchmarks, including VideoMMMU and VSI-Bench, and general video benchmarks such as MVBench and TempCompass. Video-R1-7B reaches 37.1% accuracy on VSI-Bench, exceeding GPT-4o in that reported comparison. The findings support adapting reinforcement learning specifically to video's temporal structure while drawing on image-based reasoning data.
neurips-2025-video-r1-reinforcing-video-.tldr: Video-R1 improves video reasoning through temporally focused reinforcement learning and training that combines image and video reasoning data.

paragraphs: Transfer learning uses information from source domains to improve learning in a target domain. This paper extends that idea to regression whose outputs are probability distributions, rather than ordinary numbers or vectors. It places those outputs in Wasserstein space, providing a framework suited to the distribution-valued nature of the prediction problem.

The authors distinguish two situations. When the informative source domains are already known, they construct an estimator and prove asymptotic convergence rates. These rates quantify how similarity between domains affects the efficiency of transfer. The guarantee therefore explicitly connects the usefulness of source information to its relationship with the target.

When the informative sources are unknown, the paper introduces a data-driven procedure designed to mitigate negative transfer, where borrowing source information harms target learning. The work combines theoretical analysis with simulations and real-world applications. Its contribution is both a framework for transferring distribution-valued predictions and a treatment of the source-selection problem that determines whether such transfer is helpful.
neurips-2025-wasserstein-transfer-learni.tldr: The paper develops transfer learning for distribution-valued regression, with convergence guarantees and a procedure designed to reduce negative transfer.

paragraphs: Removing knowledge from a language model can damage useful capabilities or leave it producing fabricated answers about the removed material. Attention-Shifting addresses this tradeoff by targeting how the model attends to information. Its objectives are to suppress unwanted factual content while preserving linguistic structure and discouraging invented completions.

The framework applies two coordinated interventions. Importance-aware suppression reduces reliance on memorized knowledge in the unlearning set. Attention-guided retention enhancement strengthens attention to semantically important tokens in data the model should retain. A joint dual-loss objective aims to localize the change even though different pieces of knowledge share internal representations.

Experiments report better preservation of model performance than state-of-the-art unlearning methods, with accuracy gains of up to 15% on ToFU and 10% on TDEC. The method maintains competitive hallucination-free unlearning effectiveness. These results support a better balance among removal, retained capability, and response reliability; the reported evidence concerns that balance rather than establishing that all hallucinations are eliminated.
neurips-2025-wisdom-is-knowing-what-not-.tldr: Attention-Shifting selectively suppresses unwanted knowledge while reinforcing retained information to improve the balance between unlearning and reliable responses.
